I checked file sizes, module gating, test distribution, and the outlines of `lib.rs` and `renderer.js`. The architecture is sound, the folders are mostly fine, and the real problems are three oversized files plus one design gap that blocks testing of the render layer.

## What's good
- **The sim/render split works.** `sim::GameSystems::step` and `gate_frozen_step` are shared by the browser loop and the headless `Simulation`, so the two can't drift.
- **Pure math is pulled out and tested natively.** `backdrop_clip.rs`, `static_geo.rs`, `drive.rs`, `editor.rs` and `audio/compose.rs` all follow this pattern.
- **Coverage on logic is strong**: about 390 unit tests, heaviest in scenario, AI and pathfinding.
- **The render scripts are better than typical e2e.** They test pixel identity and rig parity.
- **Zero native dependencies**, and generated data is checked in CI.

## Problems, in priority order

**1. `src/lib.rs` is a 3,954-line file that is almost entirely one inline `mod wasm_entry`.** It holds:
- `GameState` with 57 fields;
- a 600-line `update_game`;
- `render_world`;
- the whole `?viz` toolbox (about 800 lines of `draw_viz_*`);
- menus, settings and pause modals;
- the neon title font (`title_glyph` is about 200 lines);
- the perf module and URL parsing.

This is the obvious refactor. It is mechanical: split into `app/{mod,state,game_loop,world_render,menus,title,perf,url}.rs` and `viz/{effects,props,characters,musics}.rs`. `update_game` would then be split into input, tick, events-to-scenario and render phases.

**2. `Graphics` is wasm-only, and that makes the whole render layer wasm-only by contagion.** `camera.rs`, `level.rs`, `render*.rs` and `floor_props.rs` use no `web_sys` at all. They are gated only because they take `&Graphics`, whose host version is an empty stub.

Only `new`, `sync_size`, `width`/`height` and `flush` touch the browser. If the recorder (`cmds`, `texts`, every `draw_*`) compiled natively, you would get:
- host tests for `Camera`, which has zero today despite the zoom clamps and `floor_occlusion` plumbing;
- golden command-stream tests for `render_world`;
- a structural walk of every recorded frame against the arity table.

I think this is the highest-leverage change in the repo.

**3. The opcode table exists three times** (`mod op`, `OP_ARGS` in renderer.js, `helpers.js`) and is kept in sync by a CLAUDE.md rule. You already have `gen_levels.py` and `gen_props.py`. A `gen_ops` step, or a host test that parses `OP_ARGS` out of `renderer.js` and compares, would turn the rule into a check. The same applies to the mirrored drive/shader constants.

**4. `initRenderer` in `renderer.js` is one 2,300-line closure with 54 inner functions.** The natural seams already exist:
- shaders;
- postfx and warp;
- pixel groups;
- static cache;
- drive and backdrop;
- text atlas;
- sprite caches;
- batch.

Splitting into ES modules that share a small `ctx` object adds no dependency and no bundler, since `robot-core.js` is already imported that way.

**5. `props.rs` (5.3k lines) and `audio/engine.rs` (4.3k lines) are too large.**
- `props.rs` should be split by family (`props/{datacenter,outdoor,lobby}.rs`). `PROP_FAMILIES` already defines the boundaries.
- `engine.rs` has zero tests. I haven't read it in depth, but at that size there is likely pure synthesis or scheduling logic that could be extracted the way `sfx.rs` was.

## Folders
- **Root.** Move the JS runtime into `web/` (`renderer.js`, `robot-core.js`, `shoggoth-core.js`) only if you do the renderer split. Otherwise it isn't worth the churn to serve.py routes.
- **`tests/e2e/`.** It mixes Playwright specs with standalone render scripts. A `tests/render/` folder would match the two Makefile targets.
- **Stale docs.** `ECS_ARCHITECTURE.md` and `TESTING.md` were last touched 2026-09-02 and sit at the root while everything else is in `docs/`. Move them, and re-check them against the current code.
- **Small stuff.**
  - The `CanvasRenderingContext2d` web-sys feature is unused.
  - `components/mod.rs` is 1,082 lines in a single file.
  - `render.rs`, `render_comms.rs`, `render_dialogue.rs`, `hud_*.rs` and `floor_props.rs` would read better as a `render/` directory.

## Tests
- Playwright has only 3 tests in total. That is fine as long as the headless sim carries gameplay, and it does.
- The gaps are the ones from problem 2: camera, command-stream structure, and `editor_ui` hit-testing.
- A cheap, high-value addition is a smoke test that loads every floor in `Simulation` and runs N frames asserting no panic and no NaN. Check that `playthrough_gate.rs` doesn't already cover it.

## CLAUDE.md
It is 47 KB and loaded into every session. About 80% of it is renderer history ("measured 8.6 -> 6.8 ms…") that belongs in `docs/PIPELINE.md` or a `docs/RENDERING.md`. Keep the rules, the invariants, the "edit both or neither" list and the pointers.

## Order I'd do it in
1. Host-side `Graphics` recorder, problem 2. It is small and it unlocks the tests.
2. Opcode sync test, problem 3.
3. `lib.rs` split, problem 1. It is pure moves, and `make verify` proves it.
4. `renderer.js` modules, problem 4. `check-render` is the safety net.
5. `props.rs` by family, then the CLAUDE.md diet.

Steps 1 to 3 are low-risk. Want me to start with 1 and 2?

items.text:
I measured the test loops on this machine. Most of your points I agree with; I push back on two (the bun generator and one Playwright test per level) and retract one (my per-floor smoke test already exists).

## 2. What "wasm-only" means here

Rust can compile the same source for different targets. This project uses two:

- **native** (your Linux CPU): what `cargo test` builds and runs directly in the terminal.
- **wasm32**: the `.wasm` file the browser loads.

**What `web_sys` is.** It is the crate that exposes browser APIs (`window`, `document`, the canvas, WebAudio) to Rust. Those APIs only exist inside a browser. So any code that calls them is marked `#[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]`, which means "only compile this when targeting wasm". In a native build that code is absent, and you can't write a `#[test]` for it.

**What is actually browser-bound.** `Graphics` is a `Vec<f32>` that every `draw_*` call appends numbers to. That part is plain Rust. Only four methods touch the browser:

- `new` (finds the canvas),
- `sync_size`,
- `width`/`height`,
- `flush` (hands the Vec to JS).

Because those four need `web_sys`, the whole struct was gated. On native it is an empty stub (`pub struct Graphics;`).

**The contagion.** `camera.rs`, `level.rs`, `render*.rs` and `floor_props.rs` take a `&Graphics`, so they got gated too. None of them use `web_sys` themselves. That is about 3,000 lines of pure logic that can only be tested through a real browser.

**The fix.** Gate only those four methods. On native, `Graphics::new_headless(w, h)` records into the same Vec, and a test reads it back, for example: "render floor 3, walk the command stream, assert every opcode has the right arity and the BACKDROP occlusion rect is inside the screen".

Measured loops after touching one source file:

| Loop | What runs | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Native unit tests (`cargo test --lib`) | incremental compile, then 336 tests | **about 1 s total** (tests: 0.04 s) |
| The same after a real edit | more to recompile | about 2–6 s (estimate) |
| wasm release build only | `lto` + 1 codegen unit | **15 s** |
| `make check-e2e` | wasm build + Chromium + 3 tests | **48 s** (tests: 38 s) |
| `make check-render` | 5 scripts | about 60 s (per CLAUDE.md, not re-run) |

The cost in both loops is compiling and launching Chromium. Test execution is almost free. A render-layer bug costs about 50 s per try today and would cost about 1–5 s once it is host-testable. Native tests are also deterministic, with no timeouts and no flaky frames.

## 3. Generator: bun or Python?

This is not really a bun project. Bun is only the e2e test runner, and its `package.json` lives in `tests/e2e/`. The build tooling is Python 3 stdlib (`gen_levels.py`, `gen_props.py`, `gen-title`, `serve.py`). `make verify` currently needs only Rust and Python.

I'd use neither for the opcode table:

- **The check.** Add a Rust host test that does `include_str!("../renderer.js")`, parses the `OP_ARGS = [...]` line and compares it to `mod op`. It runs inside `cargo test`, so it is already covered by `make verify` with no extra toolchain.
- **One fewer copy.** `renderer.js` exports `OP_ARGS` and `helpers.js` imports it. That takes three copies down to two.

I wouldn't port the Python generators to bun. It would make bun a hard requirement for the core `verify`, and the gain is only consistency.

## 4. Bundling

Yes, bundling is possible, and it adds no dependency. `bun build web/renderer.js --minify --outdir dist` is a built-in bundler that handles the ES imports you already have.

I'd only bundle for deploy. Today there is no JS build step: you edit a file and refresh. `wasm-build.yml` already assembles a Pages artifact, so that workflow is where the bundle step belongs, and local dev keeps serving the source files.

The size gain is small next to the 880 KB wasm. The real benefit is a single cache-busted file. I'd do the split first and add the bundle as a small follow-up.

## 5. `props.rs` and `audio/engine.rs`

Yes, split both.

## Folders

- **What those JS files are.** `renderer.js`, `robot-core.js` and `shoggoth-core.js` are plain hand-written JS and can move to `web/`.
  - `open_miami.js` and `open_miami_bg.wasm` are generated by wasm-bindgen and gitignored. I'd leave them where the build puts them, or point `--out-dir` at `web/` too.
- **What is inside `tests/e2e/`.** Two unrelated kinds of test share that folder because they share `node_modules`:
  - `specs/*.spec.js` are 3 Playwright tests that play the real game: it loads floor 1, it kills the rogues, and it rides the lift to floor 2.
  - The 5 root scripts are renderer-only. They feed hand-built command streams to `renderer.js` and compare pixels. There is no game and no wasm involved.
  - I'd move the scripts to `tests/e2e/render/`. The `package.json` is shared, and only the grouping changes.
- **`CanvasRenderingContext2d`.** `Cargo.toml` lists which browser APIs `web-sys` should generate bindings for. This one is left over from before the WebGL renderer, and nothing in `src/` references it. Removing it is a one-line deletion with slightly less to compile.
- **Docs and `render/`.** Yes to cleaning the stale docs and to the `render/` directory. `components/mod.rs` stays as is.

## Tests: one Playwright test per level?

I'd push back on that.

- **The all-floors smoke test already exists.** `tests/playthrough_gate.rs::every_level_reaches_a_terminal_state` plays every floor headlessly with a bot and checks for NaNs, in milliseconds. My earlier suggestion of a per-floor smoke test was redundant.
- **The cost is too high for what it adds.** 15 floors in Playwright at about 10 s each is roughly 150 s, against a 60 s cap. It would mostly retest what the simulation already proves.
- **What a browser adds per floor** is JS-side render errors, such as a prop or surface the renderer chokes on. For that I'd write one spec that loops over all floors, runs about 1.5 s each, and asserts no console errors plus a well-formed command stream. That takes about 25 s.
- **Most of that moves to `cargo test` anyway.** Once point 2 lands, the "well-formed stream for every floor" check runs there in about 1 s.

## Proposed order

Each step is its own unstaged diff, with `make verify` run after each. `make verify-all` also runs after the JS and test moves.

1. Host `Graphics` recorder. Un-gate the camera, level and render modules. Add camera tests and an all-floors stream test.
2. Opcode sync test, plus `OP_ARGS` exported to `helpers.js`.
3. Split `lib.rs` into `app/` and `viz/`. Move `render*`, `hud_*` and `floor_props` into `render/`.
4. Split `props.rs` by family, then look for extractable pure logic in `audio/engine.rs` (I haven't read it closely enough to say what splits cleanly).
5. Create `web/`, split `renderer.js` into modules, move the render scripts to `tests/e2e/render/`, and add the bun bundle step to the deploy workflow.
6. Add the one all-floors Playwright spec, remove the unused web-sys feature, clean the stale docs, and trim CLAUDE.md into `docs/RENDERING.md`.

The file moves in steps 3–5 will show as delete-and-add pairs in your unstaged diff, since I don't use `git mv`. I'm starting on step 1 now.
The gated render modules have no browser dependency other than `Graphics`, so the recorder un-gating is clean. Reading `graphics.rs` in full before editing.

Steps 1 and 2 are done and verified. `make verify` passes with 348 unit tests plus the new integration tests. `make check-e2e` passes 3 of 3, and `make check-render` reports ALL PASS, so the wasm side behaves the same as before.

## What changed

**`Graphics` is now one struct with two surfaces, instead of a browser version and a PC version (your point 2).**
- Every `draw_*` method is shared Rust that compiles on both targets.
- Only the surface differs:
  - In the browser it is the canvas plus `flush`, which hands the frame to JS.
  - On native it is `Graphics::new_headless(w, h)` plus `take_frame()`, which hands the frame to a test.

**More code was gated than I told you earlier.** `camera`, `level`, `render*`, `floor_props`, the roughly 3,000-line prop drawing module, the `drive` and `ending` draw code, and `sparks` all lost their wasm gate. Only `input`, `editor_ui`, the audio engine and the browser entry point are still wasm-only.

**`src/graphics/stream.rs` (new)** holds:
- the Rust `OP_ARGS` arity table,
- a stream walker,
- a structural validator,
- a mirror of renderer.js's transform maths.

**The new tests are the payoff:**
- **Opcode sync:** `cargo test` parses `OP_ARGS` out of both `renderer.js` and `helpers.js` and compares them to the Rust table. The CLAUDE.md "keep in sync" rule is now a failing test.
- **`tests/render_stream.rs`:** all 15 floors are recorded three ways (first frame, cached frame, debug frame) and every one of the 60 props is recorded at every pixel size. All of them are validated in 0.01 s. It also proves the floor cache content does not depend on the camera.
- **Camera:** 6 tests, the first the camera has had. They check `screen_to_world` against the transform `apply()` actually records, the zoom clamps, and that the backdrop occlusion rect really lies on the floor.

## Your other points

**3. One fewer copy, and the tooling policy.**
- The policy is now in CLAUDE.md under Development Constraints: new tooling is TypeScript run with Bun, no new Python scripts, the existing Python tools stay until they need real work, and prefer a Rust host test when one fits.
- The "one fewer copy" is deferred to the renderer split. `helpers.js` is CommonJS and `renderer.js` is an ES module with imports, so a clean import needs the small dependency-free `web/ops.js` that the split will create. Until then the Rust test pins both copies, so they can't drift.

**4. Split, then bundle for deploy.** Yes, in that order.

**5. Why `robot-core.js` and `shoggoth-core.js` are JS.** They are the robot and boss renderers: 3D box models drawn with WebGL into small pixel-art tiles. They are in JS for three reasons:
- **The heavy work already runs on the GPU.** The skeleton is evaluated in a GLSL vertex shader. Per frame, JS computes about 16 pose numbers per robot, does one buffer upload and makes one draw call for all robots.
- **WebGL is only reachable through JS.** Rust in wasm cannot call the GPU directly. A Rust version would cross the wasm-to-JS boundary on every `gl.*` call, which is slower than today's single crossing per frame.
- **The tools use them without wasm.** `inspector.html` and `rig-parity.html` import `robot-core.js` directly.

The one candidate for Rust is `posePlan`, the pose logic, which would become host-testable. I'd leave it, because `rig-parity.js` already covers it and the tools would then need wasm. Splitting `robot-core.js` into smaller JS modules is reasonable and belongs with the renderer split.

## Where I stopped

I stopped at the step boundary on purpose. You sync through the unstaged diff, and step 3 (the `lib.rs` split) is thousands of moved lines that would bury this diff. Once you've picked this one up, I'll continue in the agreed order:
- Step 3: `lib.rs` into `app/` and `viz/`, plus the `render/` directory.
- Step 4: `props.rs` by family, and `audio/engine.rs`.
- Step 5: `web/`, the `renderer.js` modules with `ops.js`, `tests/e2e/render/`, and the Bun bundle in the deploy workflow.
- Step 6: the all-floors Playwright spec, the web-sys cleanup, and the docs and CLAUDE.md trim.

Step 3 is done and green: `lib.rs` went from 3,951 lines to a 52-line module list. `make verify` passes (394 tests), Playwright passes 3/3, and all five render scripts pass.

## What moved
The browser app now lives in `src/app.rs` plus `src/app/`:

| File | Lines | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `app.rs` | 673 | `GameState`, screen dispatch, floor load and checkpoints, `start()` and the rAF loop |
| `app/game_loop.rs` | 688 | `update_game`, boss intro, ending |
| `app/world_render.rs` | 291 | `render_world` |
| `app/robots.rs` | 315 | the actors layer, pose and colour tables |
| `app/menus.rs` | 485 | level select, modals, settings, about, pause |
| `app/title.rs` | 311 | the neon glyphs |
| `app/viz.rs` + `viz/{effects,props_page,musics}.rs` | 283 + 837 | the `?viz` toolbox |
| `app/url.rs`, `app/perf.rs` | 33 + 67 | URL params, `?perf` spans |

The three render modules moved to `src/render/{comms,dialogue,floor_props}.rs`; `render.rs` stays where it is.

## Proof nothing changed
- **A script did the split, not hand-editing.** It cut by line range, dedented, and bumped visibility to `pub(crate)`.

The line I'd draw is one question per module: does it need to know what happened this frame, or only what the world looks like right now? The current code does not follow that line yet. Three files in `app/` fail it, and I checked which ones before answering.

## The layers as I see them

| Layer | The question it answers | Allowed to touch | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| sim | What is the state of the world? | the `World` only | `ecs`, `systems`, `scenario`, `game`, `sim` |
| render | What does this state look like? | state (read-only) + `&Graphics` | `render.rs`, `render/*`, `level`, `camera`, the prop/drive/ending draw code |
| app | What happens this frame? | everything: input, clock, audio, settings, URL, mutable `GameState` | `app.rs`, `app/*` |
| `renderer.js` | How do commands become pixels? | the GPU | `renderer.js` and its helper JS files |

**The test for "render":** the code is a function from state to drawing commands. It reads no input, mutates nothing, and calls no browser API.
- Anything that passes can run natively. After step 1 that means it can be tested in about 1 s.
- Anything that fails is "app": which screen we're on, in what order things get called, reacting to a click, starting a sound, saving a setting.
- Menus and the `?viz` pages are immediate-mode UI, where drawing a button and reading its click are the same call. They belong in `app`, like `editor_ui`.

## Where the code doesn't match that yet

Step 3 was a pure move, so I cut by where the code already sat and not by this rule. I counted what each `app/` file actually uses:

| File | Input reads | Audio uses | State mutations | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `game_loop.rs` | 25 | 32 | 30 | app |
| `menus.rs` | 28 | 3 | 18 | app |
| `viz.rs` | 2 | 1 | 5 | app |
| `title.rs` | 0 | 0 | 0 | really render |
| `robots.rs` | 1 | 0 | 0 | really render |
| `world_render.rs` | 0 | 0 | 1 | really render |

The two leaks are small:
- **`robots.rs`.** In the middle of drawing the player, it asks "is the left mouse button down?" to choose the shoot pose. Passing in `firing: bool` fixes it.
- **`world_render.rs`.** `render_world` decrements the kill-flash timer while it draws. That decrement belongs in `update_game`, and `render_world` should only read the value.

Moving those three files into `render/` is more than tidying. Today `tests/render_stream.rs` contains `record_floor`, which is my hand-written copy of `render_world`'s draw order. If the two drift, the test keeps passing and proves nothing about the real game.

Once `render_world` and `draw_robot_entities` live in `render/` and take a plain view struct, I can do two things:
- delete the copy, so the test calls the real function on every floor;
- test for the first time the actors layer: robots, heads, poses, downed and headless states.

- fixing the two leaks;
- moving `title`, `robots` and `world_render` into `render/`;
- pointing the stream test at the real `render_world`.

The boss uses two shaders in the boss pipeline, plus a third that lives in `renderer.js`. My four steps described the work, not the shader count. Only two of those steps run on the GPU; the other two are plain JS on the CPU.

| Step | Where it runs | What it actually is |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Build the model | CPU, JS | One unit sphere mesh, made once (`makeSphere`). The boss is nothing but spheres. |
| 2. Animate | CPU, JS | Each frame, JS computes a 4×4 matrix per blob: where each lump of the mass sits, how the tentacle segments curl, how far the mask has cracked. |
| 3. Render into a texture | GPU, shader 1 | `sceneVS` and `sceneFS` in `shoggoth-core.js`, about 30 lines. JS draws the same sphere once per blob, setting a different matrix and colour each time. The code has 17 sphere and blob call sites, several of them inside loops. |
| 4. Pixelate and ink | GPU, shader 2 | `postVS` and `postFS`, inherited from `robot-core.js`. One full-tile draw reads step 3's texture, snaps it to chunky blocks and inks the outlines. |

After that, `renderer.js` places the finished tile on screen with the ordinary batch shader. That is the same shader every rect and sprite in the game goes through.

**Shader 1 is simple.** It is a lit sphere: transform the vertex, shade by the normal against one fixed light, and mix toward a glow colour. It also writes a per-part id into the alpha channel. I haven't read far enough to confirm how shader 2 uses that id.

**All the character is in JS.** The writhing, the tentacles and the mask crack are JS deciding where the spheres go each frame. The GPU only draws shaded spheres.

**The robots were deliberately moved away from this design.** Their skeleton now runs inside the vertex shader (`rigVS`), and a whole squad is one instanced draw. That matters because there can be dozens of robots on screen. There is only ever one boss, so a few dozen draws for it is cheap, and it kept the simple design.

By the test in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, the blob placement is render-layer code: it is a function from `(time, reveal, heading)` to a list of spheres. Today that function lives in JS, so it has no native tests, and a constant (`MASK_OFF_SECS`) has to be mirrored by hand.

- **The command is already minimal.** It carries 6 floats (`x y size heading reveal time`), and JS expands them deterministically. Yes. Long term I would apply one rule to both characters: Rust computes poses as numbers, GLSL evaluates the rig, and JS only carries data between them. "All Rust" and "all WebGL" are both the wrong cut.

## Why neither extreme works

- **All Rust is not possible.** The skeleton and the inking have to run on the GPU, so they stay in GLSL whatever we do.
- **All WebGL/JS is what we have now, and it has a coupling problem.**
  - Rust owns the finisher timers and the impact frames.
  - JS owns the kick and stomp keyframes, which have to line up with those timers.
  - That is gameplay choreography mirrored across two languages, and no test pins it.

What can actually move is the code in between: the function that turns `(pose, time)` into joint angles.

## The robots are already shaped for this

`posePlan(pose, time, relaxed)` is a pure function of about 150 lines. I checked it: no state, no randomness, no browser calls. It returns a small set of scalars (`bob`, `lean`, `legA`, …).

Those scalars already are the interface. The GPU rig takes 16 floats per robot (tile, facing, palette index, and the `posePlan` scalars) and does the rest in the vertex shader. So the seam already exists, currently between two pieces of JS.

Moving it is contained:
- port `posePlan` to a `render/pose.rs`;
- have the `ROBOT` op carry the scalars in place of `poseIdx + time`.

The safety net for this port is strong. Before deleting the JS version, a parity test can dump the scalars from both implementations for every pose across a sweep of times, and require them to match. After the move, the kick's foot extension and its impact time live in one language and can be checked by `cargo test`.

## The boss has no such seam yet

`shoggoth-core.js` builds a matrix per sphere on the CPU and issues one draw per sphere. There is no "pose numbers" layer to cut along.

The boss first needs the refactor the robots already had:
- draw it as instanced spheres;
- give each sphere a per-instance float block.

That refactor is worth doing anyway, since it turns a few dozen draws into one. It also creates the seam, and once the seam exists Rust can fill the instance list.

## The two costs, and how they shrink

- **Tools without the wasm.** `inspector.html` and `rig-parity.html` would have to load the wasm and call an exported `pose_plan(...)`. The wasm is already built for the game, so this is a plumbing change to the tool pages.
- **Look-dev speed.** Today a pose tweak is edit and refresh. In Rust it costs a rebuild: 15 s in release mode, probably a few seconds with a dev-profile wasm build, which I haven't measured. This cost gets smaller but does not go away.

## Order

I would do none of this now; step 6 comes first. After that:

1. Port `posePlan` to Rust behind the scalar-parity test. This is cheap, and it removes the choreography mirroring.
2. Move the boss to instanced spheres in JS, with a pixel-parity page built first.
3. Move the boss's sphere placement to Rust.
4. Make the tool pages load the wasm for poses.

Step 1 is small enough to slot in right after step 6. Steps 2 and 3 are the "not the easiest right now" part, and they can wait without harm because there is only one boss.

I can add this plan to `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` as a roadmap section, so the rule is written down before any of it is built.

Fixed. The glitch was a real bug, and you described it exactly: for one frame, neither screen was drawn.

## The cause

Every menu transition was written as `self.screen = X; return;`. It switched state and returned without drawing anything that frame.

- **Title to SETTINGS or ABOUT, and back:** the frame held only a `CLEAR`. I measured 5 floats in the whole command stream.
- **PAUSED to SETTINGS, back, and resume:** this case was worse. The world is recorded before the input check, so the frame held the raw world (624 floats) with no modal and no static.
- **Boss intro to the fight, and credits to the title:** these had the same pattern.

Each screen now records the intent, draws itself fully, and only then switches. That covers ten transition sites in the menus, plus the boss intro and the credits.

I did not re-dispatch to the new screen within the same frame. The early `return` existed so the next screen wouldn't see the same key press. Re-dispatching would make Esc pause and un-pause in one frame.

- **The `ROBOT` op now carries the pose as numbers.**

  - That is 18 args. It used to be `poseIdx + time`.

- **`render/robots.rs` calls `pose_plan`.**
  - The renderer unpacks the scalars with `planFromScalars`.

- **`renderer.js` lost its `ROBOT_POSES` table.** That is one fewer table mirrored across the boundary.
- **The scalar order is a single list.**
  - `POSE_SCALARS` in `web/robot-core.js` drives the renderer's unpack and the fixture's columns.

  - `make check-pose` proves the unpack inverts it.
  - No hand-written order is left anywhere.

The render suite failed after the arity change, on a precondition check in `grain-fold`. Its pixel comparisons were not the problem.

Boss step 2 is done and sits on top of R3 in the same unstaged diff. `make verify` passes (412 tests), Playwright passes 20/20, and all six render scripts pass, including the new `shoggoth-parity`.

## What changed

- **One choke point made this possible.** Every sphere the boss draws already went through `_sphere(model, colour, accent, id, emission)`. A sphere is now 20 per-instance floats: the model's three rows plus two colour vec4s.
- **A boss frame is now two instanced draws.** The body is drawn with the depth test on, then the mask assembly with it off, in submission order.
  - It can't be one draw, because the mask is drawn depth-off on purpose so that it always sits over the lobes.
- **The original per-sphere path stays as the reference.** `pipe.instanced = false` selects it, and it is also the fallback when the instancing extension is missing. This mirrors the robots' CPU rig.
- **A detail I checked instead of assuming.** The boss's "normal matrix" is just the model's upper 3×3, not an inverse-transpose. The look was tuned with that, so the instanced shader derives it the same way.

## A number I got wrong earlier

I told you the boss was "a few dozen draws". I measured it on the parity page:
- the per-sphere path submits up to 227 draws a frame, 124 on average, each with six uniform uploads;
- the instanced path submits 2.

## The boss's first pixel test

- **What runs it.** `tools/shoggoth-parity.html` plus `tests/e2e/render/shoggoth-parity.js`, which is now part of `make check-render`.
- **What it renders.** The whole mask-off arc across a spread of clocks and headings, plus the orbit camera, the wander drift and the fine tessellation. Every frame goes through both paths at the game's exact tile settings.
- **Result.** 45 frames with 0 differing pixels.
- **What it asserts:**
  - at most 2 scene draws per frame;
  - no GL errors;
  - no instancing divisor left set on the context, since a leaked divisor would corrupt whatever the renderer draws next.
- **Mutation tests.** A zero-diff result looked too good, so I tried two mutations:
  - shifting the spheres;
  - drawing the mask with the depth test on.
  
  Both fail the test.

`all-floors` loads floor 14 but never gets past the intro card, so no test was drawing the boss through the game's own renderer. My first screenshot attempt had the boss off-camera and culled, so it proved nothing.

I redid it with the boss in frame and an op counter running:

- the boss looks right both masked and mid mask-off;
- the robots, floor and HUD text drawn around it are untouched.

The instance list is now the seam: Rust would fill those 20 floats per sphere. The matrix maths is a contained port. The part that needs a decision from you is the inspector.
